summary: This best current practice describes procedures for maintaining the Time Zone Database, which protocols such as calendaring and DHCP rely on. The volunteer who coordinated it planned to step down, so it sets up how it continues.

eli5.summary: Clocks around the world depend on a shared list of time zone rules. This explains who looks after the list and how changes are made.

questions: who maintains the time zone database
how are tz database changes decided
subtitle: Who looks after the Time Zone Database, how changes get made, and how a new maintainer is chosen.

tldr.problem: The Time Zone Database, used by protocols such as DHCP and calendaring, was kept by volunteers coordinated by one person who was about to retire.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC documents existing practice: a TZ Coordinator acting as an IANA Designated Expert, a public mailing list, update criteria, an appeals path to the IESG, and signed releases hosted by IANA.
tldr.outcome: Maintenance can continue and be handed over cleanly, with the database and code remaining in the public domain.

today: RFC 6557 is a Best Current Practice (BCP 175) and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It remains the documented procedure for maintaining the TZ Database.

sections.title: Why the Database Needed a Process
sections.content:
Time zone names are used in DHCP to configure devices with the correct local time (RFC 4833) and can appear in the TZID field of calendaring events (RFC 5545). The normative reference for these values is the TZ Database, with both historic and current entries for places throughout the world. A reference implementation of C and POSIX time functions goes with it.

From the early 1980s through 2011 the database was hosted at the U.S. National Institutes of Health. It is updated approximately twenty times per year. Arthur David Olson had maintained it since its inception, and with his retirement approaching, the time zone community asked the IETF to adopt its maintenance. The stated intent is to document existing practice and ease succession.
sections.eli5: Many devices read the same list of time zone rules. The person who kept it was retiring, so a plan was needed to keep it going.

sections.title: Roles and Terms
sections.content:
The TZ Coordinator is the person or people who maintain the database and manage its releases and the mailing list. The Coordinator is an IANA Designated Expert, except as regards appeals. There SHALL be a single lead individual and at least one backup individual, and the Coordinator also leads work to develop service metrics.

The TZ mailing list is the forum where matters about the database and supporting code are discussed. In this RFC, IANA is a role, not an organization, and its duties are provided by ICANN under the IETF-ICANN memorandum of understanding (RFC 2860).
sections.eli5: There is one main keeper of the list, with a helper, and a public chat group where people talk about changes.

sections.title: The Mailing List and Making Updates
sections.content:
The list moved from the NIH to the IANA mail server at tz@iana.org. It is used as before to discuss and confirm changes and to announce new versions. Participants are told that all their contributions are released to the public domain.

The TZ Coordinator decides changes and release timing as designated expert, but SHOULD take into account views on the mailing list. Releases SHOULD be cryptographically signed using well known public keys and distributed from the IANA site.

The criteria for updates are that new TZ names are only created when the scope a name was envisioned to cover is no longer accurate. A new name MAY be added to correct a historical inaccuracy, usually not when the inaccuracy was prior to 1970. Changes to existing entries SHALL reflect the consensus on the ground in the region.

The Coordinator SHALL NOT set time zone policy for a region. The job is to judge what the average person on the street would think the time actually is, or was.
sections.eli5: The keeper listens to the group, then decides. The keeper reports what people in a place really use for their clocks and does not decide it for them.

sections.title: Choosing a Coordinator and Handling Appeals
sections.content:
A new Coordinator is needed if the current one retires, is unable to continue, is missing, incapacitated or has died, or is not performing the function in line with community wishes. The community tries to reach rough consensus on a candidate on the mailing list, with help from the Applications Area Directors if needed. The candidate is presented to the IESG for confirmation. If consensus cannot be reached, the IESG chooses a candidate by whatever means it has.

For appeals, a person first tries to resolve the concern with the Coordinator, then seeks rough consensus on the list. As a last resort the person can appeal to the IESG, and must show that the decision was materially in error and has caused material harm.
sections.eli5: If the keeper leaves, the group suggests a new one and the top committee approves. If you disagree with a decision, you talk to the keeper first, then the group, and only then the committee.

sections.title: Reference Code and Database Ownership
sections.content:
The maintainer of the database also maintains reference code, most of which is public domain. The reference implementation shall be distributed with a cryptographic signature verifiable by a public key. Several files are distributed under license, and where they exist, licenses SHALL NOT be changed.

The database is not an IETF Contribution or document. It is in the public domain and is intended to remain so, so BCP 78 and BCP 79 do not apply to it. ICANN and the IETF Trust make no ownership claims on the database or the code, and anyone contributing waives all rights to future claims.
sections.eli5: The list belongs to everyone. Nobody can claim to own it, and anyone who adds to it gives up any claim.

sections.title: What IANA Provides
sections.content: The IANA actions are assistance when the IESG selects a Coordinator, a repository for the database and reference code, access and tooling for the Coordinator as long as no direct software costs are incurred, and security of the system hosting the database. Current and historical versions are stored and distributed via HTTP/HTTPS. IANA also keeps a private signing key that survives a change of Coordinator.
sections.eli5: IANA offers a safe home for the list and a signing stamp that stays the same even when the keeper changes.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: Distribution of the database was not secured when the RFC was written. The memo states that the TZ database SHOULD be distributed with a valid cryptographic signature from then on.
sections.eli5: Releases used to come with no proof of who made them. Now they should carry a signature so people can check them.
